claims.claim: Jenny Turner's 2001 LRB essay dismisses Tolkien's prose style in passing without analysis.
claims.source: Jenny Turner 2001, as reported in Curry, 'The Critical Response to Tolkien's Fiction'

claims.claim: The reader's impression of archaicity comes partly from over-use of nineteenth-century fiction words, avoidance of modern-world words, and dense coinages, unusual grammar and rare or obsolescent words.
claims.source: Dirk Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a stylist: a corpus-based investigation into The Lord of the Rings' (CL2017)

claims.claim: Keywords shared with nineteenth-century novels cluster in landscape, position/direction (whither, thither, thence, yonder, afar), warfare, and descriptive verbs/adjectives, many obsolete when Tolkien wrote.
claims.quote: so many of the keywords used to describe its settings

claims.claim: Tolkien borrows words such as valour, valiant and corslet from his Beowulf translation and stretches them beyond their Old and Middle English range.
claims.quote: Tolkien borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf

claims.feature: modern words in old grammatical patterns
claims.claim: Even core modern words are used in nineteenth-century patterns, e.g. 'a black smoke' with the indefinite article, rare in modern fiction.
claims.quote: tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns

claims.claim: Tolkien follows a modernist tendency in his abundant manner-laden verbs: clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glimmer, loom, peer, plod, stride, twist.
Words key only to Tolkien (dingle, fen, glades, starless, lore-masters, wolf-riders, yesteryear, yuledays, along/among/outwards) are rare but not archaic and together create otherworldliness.
claims.quote: an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness

claims.claim: Tolkien prefers the most homely collocations available yet uses everyday adjectives like 'great' in unusual pairings, and his key semantic domains (speed, size, loudness) point to hyperbole.
claims.quote: a marked preference for the most homely collocations available

claims.claim: Far from amateurish, the prose deploys several centuries of linguistic development, putting old words to new uses and vice versa.
Keyword, n-gram and collocation methods show the style of The Lord of the Rings relies heavily on nineteenth-century novels and on Tolkien's Beowulf translation.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'Tolkien as a Stylist: Key Words and Key Collocations' (2021), ch. 2
claims.quote: relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel

claims.claim: The full subtlety of Tolkien's collocations has escaped both casual readers and literary critics.
claims.quote: escaped both the casual reader's and the literary critic's notice

claims.claim: The third-person narrator presents the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, recorded in ordinary language.
Other passages carry an archaic diction reminiscent of ancient epic and Macpherson's Ossian, conveying an omniscient point of view tied to epic characters like Aragorn.
claims.quote: archaic diction, reminiscent of ancient epic poetry

claims.claim: Limiting point of view to certain characters' perceptions, thoughts and feelings follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice.
Thomas calls the narrator of The Lord of the Rings self-effacing, unintrusive and vanishing, and counts ten different viewpoints in the opening chapter.
claims.source: Paul Edmund Thomas, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators' (2000), as quoted in Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, ch. 4

verdicts.trueWording: Turner mentions Tolkien's "dreadful prose style" in passing (cf. Drout 2004)
verdicts.note: Curry PDF (raw, pypdf text, p.6): 'Turner mentions Tolkien's "dreadful prose style" in passing (cf. Drout 2004)'. Every limb held: Curry names the 2001 London Review of Books article by its editor Jenny Turner ('Reasons for Liking Tolkien', LRB 23.22, 15 Nov 2001, in the bibliography) and characterises the essay as seeking 'not so much to understand Tolkien or his readers as to place them beyond serious consideration'. 'Without analysis' is the page's 'in passing' (Curry's cf. Drout 2004 points to the analysis Turner does not do).

verdicts.trueWording: impression of archaicity ... partly due to three simple lexical causes
verdicts.note: Siepmann CL2017 PDF p.2: 'the impression of archaicity which any reader will experience on reading Lord of the Rings is partly due to three simple lexical causes: the "overuse" of words borrowed from nineteenth-century fiction, the avoidance of words associated with the modern world, and the comparatively dense use of new coinages, unusual grammatical patterns, rare or obsolescent words.' All three causes match the claim exactly.

verdicts.trueWording: four lexical sets; setting keywords 'obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing'
verdicts.note: Siepmann p.2 lists 'four lexical sets: (1) landscape description; (2) position or direction; (3) warfare and the struggle between good and evil; (4) other descriptive verbs and adjectives', among 'the highest scoring 200 key words shared with nineteenth-century novels', with 'whither, thither, thence, whence, upwards, yonder, afar' all present. The obsolescence limb is the page's 'so many of the keywords used to describe its settings were obsolete or obsolescent at the time of writing' — stated of the setting keywords, which is enough to support the claim's hedged 'many'.

verdicts.trueWording: borrows a host of words from his Beowulf translation, stretching them creatively
verdicts.note: Siepmann p.2: 'Tolkien borrows a host of words from his translation of Beowulf (e.g. valour, valiant, corslet), stretching them creatively to cover a wider range of uses than was possible in Old or Middle English'. Exemplars and the Old/Middle English range limb both verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: smoke commonly preceded by the indefinite article; 'a black smoke swirled in the air'
verdicts.note: Siepmann p.2: modern key words 'are usually part of the core vocabulary of present-day English ... However, Tolkien tends to use many of these words in nineteenth-century patterns. One example among many is smoke, which is commonly preceded by the indefinite article in Lord of the Rings (e.g. … a black smoke swirled in the air.), a use that is notably infrequent in modern fiction.'

verdicts.trueWording: follows modernist tendencies in his abundant use of descriptive verbs
verdicts.note: Siepmann p.2: 'One area in which Tolkien tends to follow modernist tendencies is his abundant use of descriptive verbs (i.e. verbs which apart from denoting an event contain an additional semantic feature that assumes the function of a manner adverb...)'. All ten verbs cited in the claim (clutch, cower, flicker, gleam, glimmer, loom, peer, plod, stride, twist) appear in the paper's key-verb list.

verdicts.trueWording: rare in present-day English, 'although not archaic', creating medievalism or otherworldliness
verdicts.note: Siepmann pp.2-3: the Tolkien-exclusive ('non-key in 19th and 20th century fiction') keywords include dingle, fen, glades, starless, lore-masters, wolf-riders, yesteryear, yuledays and 'along, among, outwards'; 'most of these words are comparatively rare in present-day English and, although not archaic, work together to create an atmosphere of medievalism or otherworldliness.'

verdicts.trueWording: homely collocations, yet 'everyday adjectives in ... unusual collocations'; hyperbole hypothesis
verdicts.note: Siepmann p.3: 'Tolkien shows a marked preference for the most homely collocations available. However, Tolkien also uses everyday adjectives in what would have been considered unusual collocations even in his day. Great, for example...' and the domains 'speed:fast (slow)', 'entire/maximum', 'sound:loud', 'temperature:hot/on fire', 'long, tall and wide' are 'the last five domains lending additional weight to the hypothesis that Tolkien tends to resort to hyperbole' — covering speed, loudness and size.

verdicts.trueWording: far from 'amateurish' ... employs several centuries' worth of linguistic developments
verdicts.note: Siepmann p.3: 'far from being "amateurish", Tolkien's prose effectively employs several centuries' worth of linguistic developments, putting old words to new uses and vice versa. In a much less obvious sense than in the case of James Joyce or Virginia Woolf, he is a linguistic postmodernist.' Quote verbatim; every limb of the claim on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: key word method, key n-grams and collocations; relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel
verdicts.note: link.springer.com serves a CDN 'Client Challenge' and has no Wayback capture for _2; recovered via Springer's own mirror host rd.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-69299-5_2 (HTTP 200, 93KB, full chapter landing page with abstract). Abstract: 'Using a variety of corpus-linguistic tools and approaches, such as the key word method and the computation of key n-grams and collocations, we show how the style of The Lord of the Rings relies heavily on the nineteenth-century novel and on Tolkien's translation of Beowulf.' Raw page reached, not a snippet or summarizer.

verdicts.trueWording: full subtlety of the resultant collocations has so far escaped ... notice
verdicts.note: Same rd.springer.com raw page (ch. 2 abstract): 'The full subtlety of the resultant collocations has so far escaped both the casual reader's and the literary critic's notice.' Quote verbatim; the claim's 'Tolkien's collocations' is the abstract's 'the resultant collocations' (those of his style, as analysed).

verdicts.trueWording: narrator presents the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits
verdicts.note: Live Springer blocked (Client Challenge); recovered via Wayback raw capture web.archive.org/web/20251019112825id_/...69299-5_4?error=cookies_not_supported. Ch. 4 abstract: 'This chapter examines those parts of The Lord of the Rings which are written as a third-person narrative. Most of the time the narrator presents the point of view of a group of characters, usually hobbits, or a single character...' and 'While the hobbits' points of view are recorded in "ordinary" language'. Both limbs on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: archaic diction, reminiscent of ancient epic poetry as well as Macpherson's Ossian
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture of ch. 4 abstract: 'other passages are characterised by an archaic diction, reminiscent of ancient epic poetry as well as Macpherson's Ossian. They convey an omniscient point of view, usually in connection with "epic characters" like Aragorn.' Every limb (Ossian, omniscient POV, Aragorn) verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: In limiting the point of view to the perceptions, thoughts and feelings of certain characters
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture of ch. 4 abstract: 'In limiting the point of view to the perceptions, thoughts and feelings of certain characters, Tolkien follows nineteenth-century novelistic practice.' Quote verbatim, whole claim supported.

verdicts.trueWording: calling him 'self-effacing', 'unintrusive' and 'vanishing' ... ten different viewpoints
verdicts.note: Same Wayback raw capture of ch. 4 — the page exposes the chapter's Notes; note 7 reads: 'Paul Edmund Thomas draws attention to the narrator's non-committal stance in the opening chapter, calling him "self-effacing", "unintrusive" and "vanishing" (175-176), and identifies ten different viewpoints in this first chapter (177).' The Works Cited on the same page confirms Thomas, Paul Edmund, 'Some of Tolkien's Narrators', in Tolkien's Legendarium (Greenwood, 2000), 161-181. All limbs verbatim.
